summary: An April 1st joke RFC proposing Mostly Pointless Lamp Switching, an architecture for carrying electricity over IP with an MPLS control plane. It parodies telecom marketing and is not a serious proposal. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke imagines sending electricity like data over an IP network. It uses networking terms to describe light bulbs, power lines, and electricity routing.

questions: how does rfc 3251 imagine electricity over ip
subtitle: An April 1st joke about carrying electricity over IP with an MPLS control plane.

tldr.problem: The RFC humorously claims that electricity distribution should use IP instead of what it calls a legacy distribution system.
tldr.mechanism: It invents Mostly Pointless Lamp Switching, encoding voltage and current into bits and using labels and signaling to route electricity.
tldr.outcome: This April 1st document is satire about applying networking concepts to electricity, not an implementable power-grid design.

today: RFC 3251 is an Informational April 1st joke document proposing the fictional MPLampS architecture.

sections.title: The MPLampS Premise
sections.content:
The RFC introduces Mostly Pointless Lamp Switching (MPLampS), an imagined way to carry electricity over IP with an MPLS control plane. It openly frames the document as a template for complicated and unimplementable “foo-over-MPLS” proposals.

Its terminology renames lamps as Low-voltage Electricity Receptors and electricity sources as generators. The memo's key words, it says, do not mean anything.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo pretends that electricity could be routed like Internet packets. Its made-up names and stated purpose show that it is a joke.

sections.title: Encoding and the Imagined Network
sections.content:
The RFC says a source would encode voltage and current into a bit stream and a destination would decode it. It equates voltage with an MPLS label and treats switching elements and transformers as Load-Switching Routers.

Its lamp example has a switch request an electricity path using RSVP-TE; a response sets up label mappings and electricity then flows. The RFC admits that this description is vague and sounds crazy.
sections.plainLanguage: In the imagined system, a power source turns electricity into bits. Routers set up a labeled path to a lamp, then a decoder recreates the voltage and current.

sections.title: Multicast and the Satire
sections.content:
The memo jokes that neighboring lamps are likely to turn on together and proposes multicast to reduce signaling. It invents names for protocols and describes electricity delivery to groups of lamps.

It closes by calling the architecture a high-visibility placeholder with many missing details. The security section says to keep the document in a locked cabinet so it is not thrown away.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC extends the joke with group delivery of electricity and more invented protocols. Its deadpan warnings and admitted lack of detail are part of the satire.
